lesson.menu_title: The Extent to Which — Taking an Argument Apart
lesson.menu_desc: A dense opinion piece, four studies and the one sentence the whole thing rests on -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- The Extent to Which
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Henrique Monteiro Neto | Lesson 14 -- The Extent to Which

listenings.text: Before you decide whether you agree, do this. Find the sentence the argument rests on. It is almost never the conclusion, it is frequently in the middle, and in about one case in five it is in a footnote. Second thing, and this one surprises people. A strong opening is not evidence that the rest is strong. It is the opposite of a guarantee. A watertight first section earns trust, and trust is exactly what a weak third section spends. So read the beginning generously and the middle suspiciously. And here is my test for a leap. Two facts, both true, and the second presented as a consequence of the first. Ask two questions. Is a mechanism proposed by which one produces the other? And does the author say, in their own words, that they are making an inference? If the answer to both is no, you have found the place where the argument stops being an argument.

I want to defend him, up to a point, and I will start by giving away the strongest objection. Paragraph six does not follow. He should have written one sentence saying that he was inferring rather than reporting, and he did not, and that is a real fault. Now the defence. If we require a demonstrated mechanism for every inference in a piece of this length, nothing gets written at all, and the journals fill up with papers that establish nothing carefully. As for the four studies using four definitions, I would ask you to name me a field in which any two studies use identical definitions. There is no such field. Pointing that out is not a finding, it is a description of research, and a review that treats it as a discovery is doing something rather like what it accuses him of.

extra_audio.text: Elif says she teaches one habit: find the sentence the whole argument rests on. He observes that in this piece that sentence is in a footnote. She calls it careless rather than deliberate, and says that is the more interesting case. He returns to the four studies, none of which defines the term the same way. She says she would tell the author that paragraph six is a leap he is entitled to make and obliged to declare.

paras: The article is a good one, which is what makes it worth taking apart. It is well written, it cites four studies, and its author is somebody whose earlier work I have quoted approvingly. The first two sections are watertight. That is precisely why the third one works on the reader: by the time the leap arrives, the piece has earned enough trust to be believed without being checked.

The argument rests on a definition given in a footnote, and the extent to which everything depends on that footnote is never acknowledged. Four studies are cited, none of which uses the same definition as the other three, and two of which were designed to answer a different question altogether. That is not dishonesty. It is what happens when a writer knows a field well enough to stop noticing that its terms are contested.

The central move is in paragraph six. Two facts are established, both of them true, and the paragraph then treats the second as a consequence of the first. It does not follow. There is a mechanism by which it might, and the author does not propose one; there is a counterexample from the same decade, and it is not mentioned. Unpack the sentence and it contains three separate claims, of which only the first is supported.

None of this makes the conclusion wrong. It may well be right, in which case somebody will have to argue for it properly. What the piece does is present as demonstrated something that remains, at best, a reasonable inference — and it does so in a register so calm and so well sourced that disagreeing with it feels like pedantry rather than reading.
